html:
The early Tibetans were the peoples of the Tibetan Plateau, the highest inhabited land on Earth, shown on the map from about 1500 to 700 BCE. They were the ancestors of the Tibetans, who speak a branch of the Tibeto-Burman languages.

People had visited the plateau for tens of thousands of years, and the earlier Denisovans had lived on its edge even before modern humans. But living there all year round, above three thousand metres, became common only after about 1600 BCE, when farmers brought barley, a crop that can stand the cold, along with sheep. Modern Tibetans carry a gene that helps them cope with thin air, and it seems to have come from Denisovan ancestors.

There is no writing from this time. Later the kingdom of Zhangzhung rose in the west, and the Yarlung kings in the south founded the Tibetan Empire in the 600s. See also the later page on Tibet.
